list.listitem: For patients of reproductive age with irregular menses, order/perform a pregnancy test, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and serum prolactin levels, and an endometrial biopsy in those older than 45 years. C

Consider endometrial biopsy in patients <45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) if they have unopposed estrogen exposure, failed medical management, risk factors for endometral hyperplasia/cancer, or persistent AUB. B
Evaluate adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and patients with other signs of clotting problems for a bleeding disorder. B
Transvaginal ultrasound should be obtained as the first-line diagnostic test for postmenopausal bleeding. C

Options for medical treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding include IV estrogen, combined oral contraceptives, tranexamic acid, levonorgestrel intrauterine device (LNG-IUD), NSAIDS and oral progestins. B

For those with symptomatic uterine fibroids, contemporary gonadotropin releasing hormone antagonists (elagolix, relugolix, linzagolix) with hormonal add-back therapy and vilaprisan, a selective progesterone-receptor modulator, are good choices for medical treatment. A
Options for patients with anovulatory bleeding include combined hormonal contraceptives, cyclic progestins, or LNG-IUD. B

For patients with postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial atrophy or proliferation can be treated with hormone therapy (HT) and endometrial hyperplasia can be treated with cyclic or continuous progestins, including LNG-IUD. C
The LNG-IUD is the most effective initial treatment for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding and reduces blood loss by approximately 90%; it is recommended as first-line treatment by NICE. A

Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is a term used to describe any deviation from the normal menstrual cycle. The average menstrual cycle lasts 29 days (21-35 days) with menstrual bleeding episodes lasting an average of 4 days (2-8 days). Older terms that have been used to describe AUB are: Menorrhagia: Prolonged/excessive regular bleeding Oligomenorrhea: Bleeding at intervals of greater than 35 days Metrorrhagia/Intermenstrual bleeding: Bleeding between regular cycles Postmenopausal bleeding: Bleeding at more than 1 year after menopause or at unanticipated times while taking HT after menopause

Clinically, Heavy Menstrual Bleeding (HMB) is defined by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) as an excessive menstrual blood loss which interferes with the patient’s physical, emotional, social and material quality of life.

The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) and the American College of Obstetrician-Gynecologists have endorsed a classification system using the mnemonic PALM-COEIN. The classification system divides the etiology of AUB into structural and non-structural causes (). Many terms used in the past such as dysfunctional uterine bleeding are no longer recommended.
AUB has a prevalence rate of 10% to 30% among patients of reproductive age.

Based on menstrual data from 18,875 participants from the Apple Women's Health Study (November 2019 through July 2021), the prevalence of AUB was 16.4% (n=3103; 95% CI 15.9-17.0) after accurate tracking was confirmed. Among these patients, 2.9% had irregular menses (95% CI 2.7-3.1), 8.4% had infrequent menses (95% CI 8.0-8.8), 2.3% had prolonged menses (95% CI 2.1-2.5), and 6.1% had spotting (95% CI 5.7-6.4).
Among pre-menopausal patients with AUB, authors of a systematic review including 14 studies found highly variable prevalence rates of about 3% to 24%, with higher rates among those age 45-50 years.

Author of a systematic review of 16 papers found prevalence estimates of adenomyosis among symptomatic women (e.g., menorrhagia, irregular bleeding, infertility) of 20% to 88.8%, with most diagnosed between the ages of 32 years and 38 years.

The prevalence rate of endometrial cancer is approximately 10% in patients with postmenopausal bleeding; approximately 90% of individuals with endometrial cancer will present with postmenopausal bleeding.
Caucasians have a 2.8% lifetime risk of developing endometrial cancer, compared with 2.5% lifetime risk for African Americans.

Based on data from the 2016 US Nationwide Emergency Department Sample, there were 1.03 million AUB-related visits, of which 11% resulted in inpatient admission. Predictors of inpatient admission included older age, higher income, better insurance, presentation to private hospitals and rural residence.
Excluding pregnancy-related causes, which are not covered in this chapter, the many causes of AUB can be classified into 2 major categories: structural and nonstructural ().

Structural causes are are signified by the mnemonic PALM (Polyps, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy & hyperplasia). Non-structural causes are signified by the mnemonic COEIN (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet Classified).

Authors of a systematic review of causes of AUB identified 8 papers, the largest study including approximately 60,000 first-time patients (result indicated in parentheses). The reported range of prevalences according to this classification system were:
Polyps: 1.8 to 25.6% (5.8%) Adenomyosis: 4.9-23.5% (7.8%) Leiomyoma: 12.4-55.5% (14.4%) Malignancy: 1.9-16.1% (3.4%) Coagulopathy: 0-5.6% (0.2%) Ovulatory dysfunction: 4.9-57.7% (37.7%) Endometrial: 1.6-12.8% (12.8%) Iatrogenic: 0.5-15.7% (3.9%) Not yet Classified: 0-36.1% (17.5%)

Among adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 papers including 2770 patients found the most frequent causes were ovulatory disorders (23.7%, 95% CI 22-25.5%), coagulation disorders (19.4%, 95% CI 17.8-21.1%), and platelet disorders (6.2%, 95% CI 5.3-7.3%). No cause was identified in 45.9%. An underlying bleeding disorder (Von Willebrand’s, factor XI and factor VII deficiencies) was found in 20% of patients of median age 42.5 years referred for heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) in another study.

Based on a meta-analysis of 6 studies including 1385 patients, patients with a cesarean scar defect were more likely than those without to experience AUB (RR 3.5, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.0-6.0). The bleeding pattern described by these patients was prolonged menstruation and early-cycle intermenstrual bleeding. In a second meta-analysis including 1183 patients with cesarean scar defects, the prevalence of abnormal uterine bleeding was approximately 0.46 (95% CI: 0.27-0.64).

Pelvic structural pathology causes bleeding by distortion of the endometrial cavity (fibroids), presence of endometrial tissue in the myometrium (adenomyosis), protrusion of endometrium (polyps), or because of abnormal friable tissue (cancer).

Authors of a systematic review of AUB in patients with uterine fibroids found evidence of aberrant angiogenesis with increased endometrial expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and adrenomedullin in patients with fibroids.

Although the pathophysiology of adenomyosis is unknown, activation of immune cells (e.g., increased number of endometrial lymphocytes and macrophage populations) and release of immune soluble factors as well as anti-inflammatory or regulatory mediators (e.g., elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, interferon, and tumor necrosis factor) are associated factors.

Systemic conditions and other factors (e.g., weight changes) can cause bleeding from coagulopathies, unopposed estrogen (e.g., polycystic ovarian syndrome), or disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.
Medications and herbal supplements that are associated with AUB are shown in .
A pregnancy test should be obtained on all of reproductive age with AUB. TSH and serum prolactin levels should be obtained in those with irregular menses.B
Evaluation of pre-menopausal patients older than 45 years should include an endometrial biopsy.B
Adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche should be evaluated for a bleeding disorder.B

A transvaginal ultrasound should be performed as the first-line diagnostic test for postmenopausal bleeding. Histologic sampling should be considered as first-line test for postmenopausal patients at high risk for endometrial cancer.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Possible missed menstrual period or recent positive pregnancy test, initial bleeding (often painless) followed by painful cramping, passage of tissue

list.listitem: In addition to exploring the timing and type of uterine bleeding, important features of the history include age, onset of menses, frequency, regularity, and duration of usual menstrual cycles, sexual history, medication and herbal supplement use.

Estimating menstrual blood loss is difficult. In a systematic review of 9 studies, use of pictorial blood loss assessment charts to assess menstrual blood loss was found to range in sensitivity from 58% to 97% and specificity from 7.5% to 95.5% with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 1.1 to 13.8 and 0.14 to 0.56, respectively. The French National College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians 2023 guideline recommends use of pictorial blood loss assessment for adolescents with heavy menstrual bleeding and for patients with AUB for whom there is diagnostic doubt using a threshold of 100 (for the Higham score) to define the types of AUB.
Clues to an infectious etiology are abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever or abnormal vaginal discharge.

Clues to a bleeding disorder include any one of the following: heavy bleeding since menarche, postpartum hemorrhage, surgical-related bleeding, and bleeding associated with dental work. Bleeding disorders should also be considered if two or more of the following symptoms are present: bruising or epistaxis more than once monthly, frequent gum bleeding, and family history of bleeding symptoms.
Clues on physical examination to a structural abnormality include an enlarged uterus (e.g., secondary to fibroid, adenomyosis) or pelvic mass.
Clues to polycystic ovarian syndrome are irregular menses and hyperandrogenism (e.g., acne, hirsutism).
In a cohort study of women with AUB, higher body mass index (BMI) was associated with endometrial hyperplasia versus proliferative endometrium (BMI 38 kg/m2 vs. 30.0 kg/m2, respectively).

Use of the Norwich DEFAB scale (Diabetes = 2, Endometrial thickness >13 mm = 1, Frequency of bleeding [recurrent = 4], Age >63 years = 1, and BMI >30 = 1) may be useful in predicting endometrial cancer among postmenopausal women with vaginal bleeding; a score more than 7 has a LR+ of 12.1. The authors suggest using a score of less than 3 with an endometrial stripe less than 5 mm to indicate no further need for testing and a score of 3 or more as indication for an endometrial biopsy.

In one retrospective study including 1837 patients with AUB who underwent endometrial sampling (12.2% of whom had endometrial cancer or atypical endometrial hyperplasia), a nomogram, created using five variables, had an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.80-0.87) for predicting endometrial cancer. These variables were: metabolic disease (OR 7.8, 95% CI 5.0-12.0), family history (OR 3.6, 95% CI 1.1-12.0), age ≥40 years (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.9-5.4), resistance index ≤0.5 (OR 8.7, 95% CI 4.3-17.7), and endometrial thickness ≥10 mm (OR 8.5, 95% CI 5.4-13.2).

In another study of 778 women with AUB, investigators created a model including BMI endometrial thickness, age, CA125, hypertension, and diabetes. This model predicted atypical hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma with a sensitivity of 87.5%, specificity of 80.7% and AUC of 0.92.

For patients reporting post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding, consider bleeding from the cervix and perform visual inspection and obtain cervical cytology if no lesion is identified. The incidence of cervical cancer in those with post-coital bleeding ranges between 3% and 11% and for intermenstrual bleeding, cervical cancer was identified in 4.7% in one study. Other more common causes of post-coital bleeding include infection, polyps, and cervical dysplasia.

Determine whether the bleeding pattern is ovulatory (regular cycle length and associated with symptoms of ovulation, such as cervical mucus change, premenstrual symptoms, biphasic temperature curve) or anovulatory (irregular bleeding with unpredictable cycle lengths); ovulatory bleeding is commonly associated with a structural abnormality.
A pregnancy test should be done for any patient of reproductive age to exclude complications of pregnancy.

For patients with heavy bleeding, a hemoglobin value should be obtained to evaluate for anemia; if you are suspicious of a bleeding disorder, obtain a platelet count and coagulation profile (e.g., PT, PTT, VWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor, platelet function analysis).

For adults with AUB (defined as heavy bleeding) who have normal ultrasound findings and are not using hormonal treatment, the French 2023 guidelines recommend a complete blood count, a coagulation work-up (pro- thrombin time, activated clotting time, and fibrinogen), and testing for von Willebrand disease (von Willebrand factor [vWF], Factor VIII, vWF activity, and vWF antigen); strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence.
For patients with an anovulatory bleeding pattern, obtain TSH and prolactin levels.
If a sexually transmitted infection is possible, test for gonorrhea and chlamydia.

If polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected (e.g., oligomenonorrhea, hyperandrogenism), the 2023 NHMRC guideline recommends obtaining TSH, prolactin, 17-OH progesterone, and FSH to exclude other likely causes. If hirsuitism is not clinically evident, serum total and free testosterone should be ordered, an, if norlmal, DHEA-S and androstenedione can be tested, but with lower specificity.

A novel cervicovaginal sampling test for detecting uterine cancer is under investigation. This WID-qEC DNA methylation test is defined as the sum of the percentage of fully methylated reference of the ZSCAN12 and GYPC regions. In a study comparing the methylation test with endometrial thickness of 4.5 mm or more on ultrasound for detecting uterine cancer in 399 patients with AUB, the former had a higher area under the curve of AUC of 94.3% (95% CI 84.7-100%) vs. 87.2% (95% CI 71.1-100) with a similar sensitivity (90.9% each) but higher specificity (92.1% vs. 79.1%, respectively).

Transvaginal ultrasound (US) is considered a first-line test by all major medical societies and the American College of Radiology (ACR) in evaluating reproductive-aged patients with AUB. It is also considered a first-line diagnostic test in evaluating patients with postmenopausal bleeding, using 4 mm as the optimal cutoff value (optimal balance between sensitivity and specificity) for the endometrial stripe (endometrial cancer rate less than or equal to 0.1%). The accuracy and interpretation differ somewhat for patients who are obese or have diabetes.

Among 258 adolescents presenting to the emergency department with AUB, 43.8% underwent pelvic US, more often for those with lower hemoglobin values. The value of US in this population was questioned as there were no significant differences in treatment choices, including admission, based on endometrial stripe measurement.

In a study of 254 patients with perimenopausal AUB, an endometrial thickness of 8 or more mm was the best cutoff for predicting endometrial hyperplasia or cancer which occurred in 7.5% and 1.2%, respectively.

Endometrial volume assessed on 3-D ultrasound compared to endometrial thickness for prediction of uterine malignancy in patients with AUB was of similar sensitivity (83% for both parameters) but more specific (75% and 69%, respectively). Doppler indices were more sensitive in the diagnosis of malignancy compared to endometrial volume (82%, 81% and 82% for vascularization index, flow index and vascularization-flow index, respectively, vs. 73%).
ACR (2020) recommends US sonohysterography or MRI without and with contrast for follow-up imaging if the original ultrasound is inconclusive or further characterization is needed.

A pelvic MRI is recommended by the French 2023 guideline for women with AUB not using hormonal treatment whose pelvic ultrasound reveals one or more type 2 (or higher) uterine fibroids, to map these fibroids before myomectomy (if the ultrasound is considered insufficient) or interventional radiology. An MRI is not recommended if ultrasound findings show polyps or adenomyosis, unless there is doubt about the diagnosis of adenomyosis.

If a greater than 4 mm endometrial stripe is seen, consider saline-infusion sonography (SIS; also called saline-infusion sonohysterography); if focal thickening is seen, consider hysteroscopy. In one study, SIS was as good as hysteroscopy in diagnosing intracavitary lesions and was better tolerated by patients. In another, 3-D SIS performed better than 2-D SIS; the former was also comparable to hysteroscopy.

The Society of Obstetrics and Gynecologists of Canada (SOGC) recommend an office endometrial biopsy as the initial assessment of the endometrium in patients over age 40 years or for those at risk for endometrial cancer rather than performing a dilation and uterine curettage.

In a retrospective cohort study of patients presenting with AUB at a tertiary care referral care center, hysteroscopic visualization was associated with increased sensitivity in identifying intrauterine pathology. For cancer diagnosis, 12 cases of confirmed or suspected malignancy were found on hysteroscopy of which only one was detected on office-based, blind endometrial biopsy.

For patients with suspected endometrial malignancy, an international committee of gynecology experts recommend hysteroscopy to allow targeted endometrial biopsy for achieving the highest diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness.
In a patient with heavy menstrual bleeding and a negative ultrasound result, a saline-infusion sonohysterography can assist in identifying polyps.

Hysteroscopy (direct visualization of the uterine cavity through an endoscope) can be helpful in diagnosing endometrial hyperplasia and fibroids. One study, however, found that the addition of hysteroscopy to endometrial biopsy for the diagnostic work-up of premenopausal women with AUB did not influence management.

However, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies found the highest sensitivity and similar specificity for diagnosis of endometrial polyps (present in 38% of women with AUB) was obtained with hysteroscopy compared to saline-infusion sonohysterography (0.92 and 0.85 vs. 0.87 and 0.86, respectively). These authors noted that the gold standard for differentiating benign from malignant polyps was hysteroscopy combined with biopsy.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommend that women older than 45 years with AUB, women with risk factors for endometrial cancer (e.g., obesity, infertility, nulliparity), and women who fail initial treatment should be considered for an endometrial biopsy.

The SOGC guideline recommends endometrial biopsy after age 40 years unless risk factors are present. In one large retrospective study, age 45 years was the suggested cutoff to perform endometrial biopsy in premenopausal patients with AUB unless irregular menstrual bleeding was present. The French guideline also recommends an endometrial biopsy in adults with AUB if endometrial thickness is >15 mm; strong recommendation, low quality of evidence.

A 2025 study found that using a cut-off of >4mm on TVUS for endometrial biopsy in postmenopausal patients with AUB may miss up to 25% of p53abn endometrial cancers due to false negative results, especially in lower BMI and Black patient.

Determine the severity of bleeding and the hemodynamic stability of the patient; if there is severe bleeding or hemodynamic instability admit the patient to the hospital for management (see algorithm in ).
Measuring menstrual blood loss is not routinely recommended by NICE for HMB.
Ovulatory bleeding is predictable with regular cycle length (21-35 days) and associated with signs of ovulation (e.g., cervical mucus change, biphasic temperature curve, premenstrual symptoms).
Anovulatory bleeding is unpredictable with inconsistent cycle lengths and often not associated with premenstrual symptoms.
Select the appropriate initial diagnostic strategy (see algorithm in ) on the basis of the patient's pattern of bleeding (ovulatory or anovulatory).
Patients who are postmenopausal should have a Pap test, TSH, pelvic ultrasound, and/or endometrial biopsy. Consider Neisseria gonorrhoeae and chlamydia testing.

Testing for von Willebrand factor antigen can be performed while already on combined oral contraceptives. This may be beneficial in women being treated for acute HMB and avoids the risk of rebleeding with stopping hormones.

Patients with AUB often face access barriers. Authors of a scoping review found that creating a multidisciplinary team, bringing services together and developing a care pathway improved service availability and management in an outpatient setting and improved affordability. Patient engagement was improved through use of decision aids during consultation.
For acute heavy uterine bleeding, IV estrogen has the most rapid onset of action; other options include tranexamic acid, combined oral contraceptives, and oral progestins.B

Based on a review of guidelines, authors found that NICE, ACOG and SOGC agree that hormonal or non-hormonal medications should be the first-line treatment modality in those with absent or minor structural pelvic pathology and bleeding disorders. Surgical management is recommended in cases of identified polyps, large fibroids or unsuccessful pharmacological treatment.

For chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, the LNG-IUD is the most effective initial treatment and reduces blood loss by approximately 90%. A For patients who prefer another method, tranexamic acid, hormones, or NSAIDS can be offered. B

For those with symptomatic uterine fibroids, contemporary gonadotropin releasing hormone antagonists (elagolix, relugolix, linzagolix) and vilaprisan, a selective progesterone-receptor modulator, are good choices. A
Despite a paucity of data on patients with anovulatory bleeding, combined oral contraceptives and cyclical progestins have both been used successfully. B
For patients with postmenopausal bleeding, treat endometrial atrophy or proliferation with HT and treat endometrial hyperplasia with cyclic or continuous progestins and monitor. C

For patients with acute heavy bleeding, after volume status is addressed, the next priority is cessation of uterine bleeding. Treatment options include intravenous IV estrogen, combined oral contraceptives (containing estrogen and progestin), tranexamic acid, and oral progestins ().
IV estrogen has the most rapid onset of action; bleeding in most patients is stopped within 5 hours. Tranexamic acid can also arrest acute bleeding.

Monophasic combined oral contraceptives (e.g., 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and 1 mg norethindrone) or medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA; 20 mg) are similarly effective for most women; bleeding stops in approximately 3 days ().

Progestins can be used for patients with ovulatory AUB. In a non-inferiority RCT including 104 women with ovulatory AUB, women were randomized to two cyclic-progestin regimens – desogestrel 150 µg/d or medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg/d - orally, administered 10 days/month for 6 months. Desogestrel was comparable to MPA for endometrial response rate (78.0% vs. 70.4%, respectively), but was less effective than MPA for menstruation normalization (acceptable bleeding rate 90.0% vs 96.6%).
In adults and adolescents with heavy ovulatory bleeding, the LNG-IUD is a first-line option. It reduces bleeding more than other options.

Authors of a Cochrane review found other options to be less effective; these included combined oral contraceptives, progestins given for 3 out of 4 weeks, danazol and tranexamic acid. Progestins given for less than 2 out of 4 weeks were least effective. In this analysis, the LNG-IUD showed comparable efficacy to ablation for reduction of bleeding at 3 months.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 11 RCTs of women with a histological diagnosis of endometrial hyperplasia found the LNG-IUD used for three to six months to be more effective than non-intrauterine progestogens at reversing endometrial hyperplasia based on moderate evidence. Low quality evidence suggests that the LNG-IUD results in fewer hysterectomies (OR 0.26; 95% CI, 0.15-0.46), more bleeding/spotting but less nausea and improved satisfaction with treatment.

Regarding LNG-IUD versus hysterectomy, a Cochrane review concluded that although hysterectomy was more effective in controlling bleeding, the LNG-IUD was comparable in improving quality of life at one year. In a systematic review, the LNG-IUD was also found to be cost-effective and associated with improved health-related quality of life to a degree similar to that of endometrial ablation or hysterectomy. In one RCT of hysterectomy versus LNG-IUD with 10-year follow-up, however, 55 women randomized to the IUD (46%) underwent hysterectomy after initial allocation, the majority within the first 5 years after study enrollment.

Two LNG-IUDs, Donasert® and Mirena®, were found to be comparable for treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding in a non-inferiority RCT for both menstrual blood loss<80 mL and decrease to ≤50% of baseline menstrual blood loss, which was achieved in 139/154 (90.3%) and 126/146 (86.3%), respectively.

In a pilot study of women with AUB attributed to adenomyosis, nearly all 30 women treated for 12 weeks with ulipristal acetate, a selective progesterone receptor modulator used for emergency contraception, had reduced menstrual bleeding at 4 weeks compared to none of 10 women on placebo; there were no differences at 6 months. In an open-label Russian study of women with adenomyosis, triptorelin, an injectable gonadotropic-releasing hormone agonist analog, was successful in reducing bleeding severity and pain.
In a meta-analysis, tranexamic acid therapy was found to reduce menstrual blood loss by 34% to 54% and improve quality-of-life parameters by 46% to 83%.

Other options include combined oral contraceptives and NSAIDs. Authors of a meta-analysis concluded that 51% of women with menorrhagia benefited from NSAIDs with a 29% reduction in menstrual blood loss. Based on a Cochrane review, NSAIDS were better than placebo for heavy menstrual bleeding; comparable to oral luteal progestogen, Progestasert, and oral contraceptives (although most studies were underpowered); but not as effective as tranexamic acid, danazol or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system.

In patients with anovulatory bleeding, if there is no evidence of thyroid disease or a prolactinoma and no evidence of pathology on endometrial biopsy (if done), bleeding can usually be controlled with combined oral contraceptives or cyclic progestin therapy (e.g., MPA 10 mg for 14 days, then off for 14 days, then repeat) (). If bleeding persists after 3 months, try a pill that is higher in estrogen (up to 35 mcg) or has a higher potency progestin.

If a patient desires amenorrhea, use an extended-cycle combined oral contraceptive (e.g., Seasonale, Jolessa, Quasense [intervals of 84-day active pills then 7-day placebo pills]) or continuous combined oral contraceptive (e.g., Lybrel [365-day active pills]). If unscheduled bleeding occurs, patients can stop the pills for 3 to 4 days to reduce bleeding days.
The management of women with polycystic ovarian syndrome is discussed elsewhere.

listitem.strong: Postmenopausal bleeding and inherited bleeding disorders

list.listitem: Patients with postmenopausal bleeding, endometrial atrophy, or proliferative endometrium can be managed with HT. Endometrial hyperplasia can be treated with cyclic or continuous progestins (e.g., MPA 10 mg or norethindrone 5 mg).

Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support use of metformin given alone or in combination with standard therapy, for the treatment of women with endometrial hyperplasia based on 4 small RCTs.
When treating individuals with inherited bleeding disorders, the same medical treatments can be used with the exception of NSAIDs.

For treatment of bleeding due to progesterone-containing contraceptives (Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, Implanon, and Nexplanon) authors of a Cochrane review found that estrogen reduced bleeding for DMPA and Norplant users. Various NSAIDs had conflicting results on bleeding; only mefenamic acid has been evaluated in clinical trials and improvement in AUB may no longer be seen four weeks after completion of treatment. A small RCT showed combined OC (150 mcg levonorgesterel and 30 mcg ethinyl estradiol) was more effective than placebo at stopping bothersome bleeding while on etonogestrel implants (Impanon/Nexplanon) during the 14-day trial, but bleeding often recurred within a few days of stopping the OCs.

Oral norethindrone 10 mg reduced the duration of prolonged uterine bleeding in the first year after placement of an etonogestrel implant. It also reduced the number of bleeding days by an average of 8 days in the first 30 days after initiating treatment. However, recurrences of bleeding were frequent and occurred earlier, on average, compared with placebo.

Similarly, a combination injectable contraception containing 25 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate and 5 mg of estradiol cypionate interrupted bothersome uterine bleeding/spotting for at least 7 days the month after receiving the intervention injection compared with placebo (87% vs 48%, respectively) based on an RCT including 46 patients. Being bleeding free at 21 days after treatment and having no recurrent bleeding at 12 weeks was reported by more participants in the intervention group, but did not reach statistical significance.

Ulipristal acetate was found to decrease the number of bleeding days in etonogestrel implant users compared with placebo in a small RCT over 30 days, with systemic progesterone levels in the nonovulatory range.

Authors of a review of 4 studies with 221 pre-menopausal women with heavy menstrual bleeding from uterine fibroids were unable to determine if the LNG-IUD was more effective than combined oral contraceptives at reducing AUB.

NICE recommends offering ulipristal acetate 5 mg (up to 4 courses) to women with HMB who have fibroids ≥3 cm in diameter and Hgb ≤10.2 g/dL, and considered for those with Hgb >10.2 g/dL. In the systematic review cited above, authors noted that treatment with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist ulipristal acetate, as well as with continuous oral contraceptives reduced several angiogenic parameters, including VEGF.

Elagolix, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist, has been found to reduce menstrual blood loss in women with fibroids according to a recent RCT, however, loss of bone mineral density is a concern and add-back hormonal therapy may be considered.

In a report of two 3-arm, industry-sponsored phase-3 trials with 790 premenopausal women with uterine fibroids and at least 80 mL of menstrual blood loss per cycle over 2 cycles, use of elagolix alone or elagolix plus add-back therapy was more effective than placebo in achieving at least a 50% reduction in blood loss from baseline to month 6 (84% and 77%.7% and 10%, respectively). Women in both intervention groups also experienced clinically and statistically significant reductions in symptom severity scores compared with women taking placebo. Adverse effects were more common with elagolix including hot flashes (43% to 64% with elagolix-alone and 20% with elagolix and add-back therapy), headache and night sweats in the elagolix-alone group, and nausea in the elagolix with add-back therapy group. The elagolix-alone group had larger decreases in bone mineral density than the placebo or elagolix with add-back therapy groups.

In an RCT including 82 patients with leiomyomas and heavy menstrual bleeding, once daily elagolix 150 mg without add-back treatment was associated with higher rates of clinical response, defined as blood loss <80 mL in the sixth month of the trial and a reduction of blood loss by at least 50%, than placebo (49% and 23%, respectively; OR 3.2 [1.1 - 9.5]).

In two 24-week manufacturer-sponsored RCTs, once-daily relugolix combination therapy (40 mg of relugolix, 1 mg of estradiol, and 0.5 mg of norethindrone acetate) reduced menstrual blood loss volume and pain in women with heavy menstrual bleeding associated with uterine leiomyomas compared to placebo (response rate 73% and 71% vs. 19% and 15%, respectively) and was well tolerated. Bone mineral density was similar for relugolix combination therapy and placebo, but decreased in the relugolix monotherapy arm.

In an extension of these trials for up to 52 weeks, 87.7% of the 163 patients treated with relugolix combination therapy who were responders, sustained improvement in heavy menstrual bleeding, had a marked reduction in Bleeding and Pelvic Discomfort scale scores (51.3 points) and had preserved bone mineral density.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs of GnRH antagonists with 2463 patients with heavy menstrual bleeding associated with fibroids concluded that, compared to placebo, the best options for bleeding suppression were elagolix 600 mg, 400 mg, and 200 mg without add-back. Elagolix 600 mg without add-back therapy had a significantly higher risk of amenorrhea than lower doses of elagolix, with and without add-back, or relugolix.

Based on a systematic review including 33 studies with a mix of RCTs and observational studies at moderate-to-high risk of bias, authors concluded that the contemporary GnRH antagonists (elagolix, relugolix, linzagolix) and vilaprisan, a selective progesterone-receptor modulator, would be the preferred oral agents for the management of symptomatic uterine fibroids due to their confirmed efficacy and milder adverse effect profiles.

For women with chronic heavy menstrual bleeding who are unresponsive to medical therapy and do not have underlying pelvic pathology, surgial options include endometrial resection with ablation, uterine artery embolization, and hysterectomy.

Endometrial ablation has an amenorrhea rate of 14% to 55%. Women considering this therapy should be finished with childbearing and use a form of permanent contraception. The procedure chosen depends on physician experience, evaluation of the endometrial cavity, and available equipment.
The Canadian guidelines recommends non-hysteroscopic ablation as the method of choice due to its higher efficacy and safety in appropriate candidates.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies including 884 women found endometrial ablation/resection and the LNG-IUD comparable with respect to satisfaction, quality of life, amenorrhea and treatment failure, and subsequent hysterectomy. Side effects, however, were less common in women treated with endometrial ablation/resection.

Compared with hysterectomy, endometrial ablation is less expensive initially with faster recovery, and fewer perioperative complications, but a repeat ablative procedure may be necessary (RR 23 at 2 years). Patients are satisfied with both procedures, but greater satisfaction with definitive hysterectomy was reported.

There are various methods used to ablate the endometrium including laser, resection, and rollerball. Newer methods have been developed that are technically easier and are performed without hysteroscopy.

Authors of a Cochrane review found newer ablative methods to be similarly effective as traditional methods (e.g., laser) with fewer surgical complications (e.g., cervical laceration, uterine perforation). Newer ablative methods were also quicker and more likely to be performed under local anesthesia.. Patients were highly satisfied with all of these procedures. Authors of a network meta-analysis found second-generation endometrial ablative systems superior to first-generation systems with some differences between second-generation systems based on outcome measured. They concluded that based on limited data, there was no convincing evidence that one second-generation system was superior to others.
In a case series of 31 patients undergoing ultrasound-guided percutaneous microwave ablation for adenomyosis, 63.3% and 65.5% achieved complete relief at 6 and 12 months, respectively.
In a case series of 242 patients with heavy menstrual bleeding, use of a single-use disposable cryoablation device resulted in reduced bleeding and improved quality of life at 12 months.

MRI guided high -intensity ultrasound, laparoscopic radiofrequency ablastion, and transcervical fibroid ablation are ablative therapy options for fibroids, with reduction in HMB not reported for MR-HIFU, 55% of patients reported reduced HMB after Lap-RFA, and 51% decrease in pictoral blood loss scores after TFA..
Uterine artery embolization (UAE)

UAE can be considered for women with symptomatic fibroids; Cochrane authors found similar overall patient satisfaction compared to hysterectomy or myomectomy and UAE offers the advantages of shorter hospital stay and quicker return to routine activities. However, the procedure is associated with a higher rate of minor complications and an increased likelihood of surgical intervention within 2 to 5 years.

In a retrospective case series of 52 patients who underwent urgent or emergent UAE procedures for AUB, 44 patients (84.6%) achieved clinical success and required no additional intervention. Diagnoses included malignancy (28.8%), post-partum hemorrhage (21.2%), fibroids (15.4%), vascular anomalies (15.4%), and post-operative bleeding (9.6%). There were no procedure-related complications reported.

Eight RCTs compared UAE with hysterectomy and myomectomy, showing similar quality of life between the treatment groups. Hysterectomy gave higher effectiveness in control of HMB, with UAE giving similar results to myomectomy, with UAE having a 42-67% reduction of HMB after 2 years, and a 10 year reintervention rate of 31%.

In this procedure, endometrial tissue is removed through loop dissection, usually under general anesthesia. Resection techniques have the advantage of destroying tissue to a known depth and provide a histologic specimen for analysis. Endometrial preparation can be conducted using a GnRH agonist one month prior to surgery.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs including 2773 women comparing hysteroscopic endometrial resection or global endometrial ablation (ER/GEA) with hysterectomy found significantly lower scores for the SF-36 general health perception, and the quality-of-life scores in social function, emotional role limitation, and vitality with ER/GEA relative to hysterectomy. Anxiety, depression scores and complication rates were similar between treatments

In one RCT of women with heavy menstrual bleeding unresponsive to progestins, hysterectomy was superior to expanded medical treatment with respect to bleeding, pain, quality of life, and sexual function.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that 58% of women randomized to oral medical therapy received hysterectomy by two years and 77% within five years; 46% of women assigned to LNG-IUD group had undergone hysterectomy by 10 years. However, urinary incontinence is more common among women treated with hysterectomy versus LNG-IUD (NNTH = 7; 95% CI, 4-266).

In a systematic review of 9 RCTs comparing hysterectomy to hysteroscopic endometrial destruction techniques, authors found that hysterectomy was more advantageous for improving AUB with high satisfaction rates and no significant decline in sexual function.

Based on nine trials comparing subtotal with total hysterectomy for benign gynecologic conditions, Cochrane authors found more ongoing cyclical vaginal bleeding up to two years after surgery for women undergoing subtotal hysterectomy, with no differences between the two surgeries in urinary, bowel or sexual function.
Danazol can be useful for patients with heavy menstrual bleeding. Limited data suggest reduced menstrual bleeding, but significant adrogenic side effects such as weight gain and acne limit its use.

Endometrial polypectomy is of uncertain benefit; there were only 2 RCTs and although the general assessment of improved/unimproved showed benefit, there was an uncertain effect on periodic blood loss.
Patients with acute heavy bleeding should be hospitalized if they are hemodynamically unstable or have severe anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL).
Patients who fail to respond to therapy after 3 cycles should be further evaluated with possible gynecology referral.
Patients with persistent endometrial hyperplasia should be referred.
In patients with acute bleeding who are hemodynamically unstable, 2 large-bore peripheral IV catheters are usually placed and volume status is corrected.
Patients should be transfused with packed red blood cells based on their hemodynamic status, degree of anemia, and wishes about receiving blood products.
Most patients (72%) with acute heavy bleeding treated with IV estrogen will stop bleeding within 5 hours. B
Most patients with AUB respond well to a LNG-IUD.B

In a retrospective study of adolescent patients admitted with menorrhagia, 92% had a decrease or cessation of bleeding regardless of which hormonal therapy the patient received; 8% required a D&C to stop the bleeding.

Once acute bleeding is stopped (whether medically or surgically), women often need medical therapy to control future bleeding; options include combined oral contraceptives, oral progestins, LNG-IUD, tranexamic acid, or NSAIDS.
Depending on age and risk factors, 1% to 14% of patients with postmenopausal bleeding will have endometrial cancer.
Individuals taking adequate iron therapy should be rechecked within 1 or 2 months; hemoglobin concentration should rise by 2 g/dL within 1 month.

Post-hormonal treatment surveillance for patients with postmenopausal bleeding found to have endometrial hyperplasia/endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia should include endometrial sampling every 3 to 6 months.
Postmenopausal patients with with an endometrial thickness <4 mm with persistent or recurrent bleeding should have histologic evaluation of the endometrium regardless of endometrial thickness.

cell.label: Assess urgency: Profuse bleeding, hemoglobin <7 g/dL, or orthostatic hypotension?
Contraindication to estrogen (e.g., estrogen-dependent tumor, thromboembolism risk, severe liver disease)?
Combined oral contraceptive (COC) 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and 1 mg norethindrone 3 times daily for 7 days.
Adequate response?
Continue with COC (once daily) or medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA; 10 mg once daily for 14-21 days per month).
Consider D&C.
MPA 20 mg 3 times daily for 10 days.
Adequate response?
Admit to hospital, monitor vital signs, place 2 large-bore peripheral IV catheters, type and crossmatch. Hemoglobin <7 g/dL?
Contraindication to estrogen?
Premarin 25 mg IV every 4 hours for up to 24 hours.
Offer blood transfusion.

algorithm.title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Management (Reproductive Aged Women).

cell.label: Rule out pregnancy. Peform pelvic exam, Pap, and strongly consider test for GC and Chlamydia.
cell.path: Pregnant, abnormal exam or Pap, or infection

cell.label: Ovulatory bleeding (menorrhagia) or anovulatory (irregular) bleeding?
Older than 40-45 years or otherwise at risk for malignancy?
Test for GC and chlamydia (if not already ordered), TSH, and serum prolactin. Consider medications as cause.

If clinically indicated, evaluate for PCOS LINK "Polycystic ovarian disease", congenital adrenal hyperplasia (early morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone), or hyperandrogenism (serum testosterone and DHEA). Yield is low, however. Consider treatment with cyclic oral contraceptive or progestin (MPA 10 mg daily for 10 days) every 1-3 months after negative pregnancy test result.
Treat underlying cause.
Order endometrial biopsy and transvaginal ultrasound with or without saline infused (sonohysterogram). Option also to do transvaginal ultrasound first and only biopsy if endometrial stripe >4 mm.
Order hemoglobin, TSH, and ultrasound. Severe bleeding, menarche, or other bleeding signs?
Cyclic oral contraceptive or, if contra-indicated, progestin (MPA 10 mg daily on days 14-28 of cycle) or NSAID for 3-4 months. Good response?
Routine follow-up.
Evaluate for coagulopathy. Abnormal?
Treat coagulopathy and correct anemia, as indicated.
Treat pregnancy, cervical abnormality, or infection. If uterus is enlarged order transvaginal ultrasound.

feature.feature_body:
Medication Dosage SORT Comments
Acute Heavy Bleeding
IV conjugated estrogen 25 mg every 4 hours for up to 24 hours B 75% of patients will stop bleeding within 5 hours
Combined oral contraceptives (monophasic)
Norethindrone 1 mg/ ethinyl estradiol 35 mcg (Necon 1/35, Ortho Novum 1/35) One pill 3 times daily for 1 week then 1pill daily for 21 days. The 21-day regiment is repeated after a 7-day interval B Most patients will stop bleeding within 3 days
Progestins
Medroxyprogesterone acetate (Provera) 20 mg orally 3 times daily for 7 days, then daily for 21 days, then daily for 21 days. Repeat 21-day regimen after 7-day interval B Most patients will stop bleeding within 3 days
Norethindrone (Aygestin) 5 mg orally 3 times daily for 21 days, repeat after 7-day interval A Most patients will stop bleeding within 3 days
Tranexamic acid (Lysteda) 650 mg 2 tabs orally 3 times daily x first three days of menses (max 5 days)or 10mg/kg IV Q8 hours A Most patients will stop bleeding within 3 daysfaster onset if given IV
Stable Heavy Bleeding
Combined oral contraceptives Daily for monthly or extended cycles A Reduces bleeding by 50% with long-term use
Progestins After stabilizing (above) B Reduces bleeding by 86% with long-term use
Medroxyprogesterone 10 mg daily for 14-21 days, monthly
Norethindrone 5 mg daily for 14-21 days, monthly
Prometrium 200 mg daily for 14-21 days, monthly A Reduce bleeding by 29%
NSAIDs
Mefenamic acid (Ponstel) 500 mg orally 3 times daily during menses
Naproxen (Naprosyn) 250-500 mg orally 2-3 times daily during menses A
LNG-IUD (Mirena) 20 mcg/24 hours for 5 years A Preferred by patients over oral progesterones. Reduces bleeding by 94%
Tranexamic acid (Lysteda) 650 mg 2 tabs orally 3 times daily x first 3 days of menses (max 5 days) A Reduces bleeding by 34%-54%
Abbreviation: LNG-IUD, levonorgestrel intrauterine device.
